SCHOTT Pharma: EPS growth restarts mostly by arithmetic and free cash flow more than doubles by FY2029, but the scope for upgrades is not yet skewed to the positive and waits for December 2027

#0 Summary of key insights, implications and conclusions

My answer to your main question: SCHOTT Pharma is not yet a situation in which upgrades are unusually skewed to the positive. The risk to estimates over the next three to six months is small, dated and largely known. The favourable gap between my view and the market's view is real, but that gap concerns free cash flow rather than earnings, and it becomes visible only in December 2027.

What the company is. SCHOTT Pharma makes the containers that injectable drugs are filled into: vials, ampoules and cartridges (the Drug Containment Solutions segment, "DCS", about 57% of sales) and prefillable syringes (the Drug Delivery Systems segment, "DDS", about 43%). SCHOTT Pharma's revenue behaves like an annuity, because a container is written into a drug's regulatory registration and 97% of revenue repeats.

Why EPS stalled, and why the stall ends. SCHOTT Pharma's EPS has sat at about EUR 1.00 for four years while revenue grew 16%. The company built capacity ahead of demand, and rising depreciation, tax and interest absorbed all of the EBITDA growth. My case for the next 12 to 24 months is that the EPS stall ends: EPS grows about 8% in FY2027 and about 10% a year after that, and free cash flow more than doubles by FY2029 once capital spending passes its FY2027 peak.

The six things that matter.

1
The FY2027 EPS turn is more reliable than the company's record suggests, because most of the turn is mechanical. About three-quarters of the swing from flat EPS to +8% in FY2027 comes from three lines below EBITDA: depreciation grows more slowly, the tax rate stops rising and the interest charge falls. EBITDA only has to grow by about EUR 20m, as it did in FY2024 and in FY2025. The market describes FY2027 as a margin-recovery year, which is a less reliable route to the same EPS.
2
Consensus EPS is a little too high, and the best-informed brokers already know it. The model's EPS is about 5% below the FactSet median for FY2027 and FY2028 (EUR 1.05 and 1.15 against 1.10 and 1.22). The three brokers with the deepest published work are at the model's numbers. The median should therefore drift down 2% to 4% after 10 December without any new disappointment.
3
Every outcome above the base case needs a capability that SCHOTT Pharma has not shown since FY2022: turning extra volume into margin while new capacity is still arriving, with no help from price. Consensus for FY2028 needs about 42 cents of extra EBITDA for each extra euro of revenue. The company has realised about 32 cents since FY2022. The model assumes 36 cents.
4
The upgrade that is available is in free cash flow, not in EPS. Consensus assumes that capital spending stays flat after FY2027. Management says capital spending falls, and management's annual bonus now rewards free cash flow. The gap between the two views shows when the company guides for FY2028 in December 2027.
5
The risk is concentrated in four places: the margin of one segment (DDS); one customer relationship (Eli Lilly, about 8% to 10% of sales); the price of renewed and new contracts from 2028; and an 18% free float that passes sector shocks through to the share price in full.
6
The model's return is large, and about half of that return comes from a higher multiple. The model gives +45.8% to 31 December 2027 at the guideline fair multiple of 23.3x. I think 23.3x belongs to a lifecycle phase that the stock has not yet earned. At 20x, my central view, the same forecasts give about +25%; at an unchanged multiple, about +19%; at the bottom-decile multiple, about -14%. The skew of returns is favourable. The skew of estimate revisions is not favourable yet.

#1 Tailwinds and headwinds in the operating environment Score 66

Bottom line. The tailwinds are strong, structural and good for volume through FY2028. The headwinds are real but concentrated in the price of new and renewed business from 2028. The operating environment therefore supports SCHOTT Pharma's growth without supplying margin.

Evidence. Three structural forces drive the EUR 3.9bn market for injectable-drug packaging, and none of the three depends on the economy: biologic drugs, obesity and diabetes injectables, and the move from bulk containers to sterile ready-to-use ("RTU") formats. Regulation adds demand and raises the barriers to entry. Customers' destocking of 2022 to 2025 is over.

The headwinds are fewer and arrive mostly from 2028. The three leading suppliers are adding syringe and RTU capacity at the same time, and prices are already giving way where capacity is loose.

Inference. The operating environment gives SCHOTT Pharma volume but no price. For SCHOTT Pharma's product mix, the environment implies growth of 7% to 8% a year from volume and mix, with like-for-like price flat.

SCHOTT Pharma's recent growth of 4% to 6% lagged the market's 9% because of vaccines and of the polymer syringes built for mRNA vaccines, which fell from about 10% of sales to about 5%. As that drag ends, the company's growth converges on the market's rate from below. The 8.3% organic growth of the June 2026 quarter overstates the trend, because it contains restocking that will not repeat. Growth driven by customers' actual use of containers is nearer 6% to 7%.

So what. Tailwinds dominate the next 12 to 18 months; headwinds dominate the debate about 2028 to 2030. External forces alone will not raise SCHOTT Pharma's margin, so each point of margin gain must come from inside the company (#2, #5).

Where I differ from the market: on the 3 November sell-off, I side with the sell-side, not with the share price. On 3 November Stevanato, SCHOTT Pharma's main competitor, cut its 2027 growth outlook because one obesity-drug maker had reduced its syringe orders. SCHOTT Pharma's shares fell 15% to 18% with no news of their own. The customer was, with high confidence, Novo Nordisk, which has lost share to Eli Lilly and is moving to multi-dose pens. About two-thirds of SCHOTT Pharma's obesity-drug revenue is with Lilly, the company that gained the share.

Stevanato's freed capacity cannot be pushed into SCHOTT Pharma's existing contracts. Changing the container supplier of a registered drug needs stability testing and a regulatory refiling, and validating a new programme takes 30 to 36 months. The pricing pressure from Stevanato's spare capacity therefore lands on awards that reach revenue around FY2029, not on FY2027 prices.

For 2028 to 2030, by contrast, I side with investors' fear over the sell-side's calm. No broker models falling prices, and the evidence for falling prices is building.

The comfort that SCHOTT Pharma is "hedged across formats" is also overstated. One monthly multi-dose cartridge at US$0.05 to 0.06 replaces four single-dose syringes at US$0.30 to 0.35 each. A patient who moves from syringes to a pen therefore stays with the supplier but takes away about 95% of the container revenue. The one available estimate, which is three years old, puts about 70% of SCHOTT Pharma's obesity-drug revenue in syringes. The format hedge protects the customer relationship, not the revenue.

Strongest counter-case: the headwinds arrive before 2028. Oral obesity drugs could take share fast (Bernstein expects oral drugs to take half the class by 2028), Lilly could follow Novo Nordisk to multi-dose pens in the United States, and the capacity overhang could repeat the post-pandemic glut in sterile filling. The evidence so far points the other way. Injections were about 90% of US prescriptions for the new obesity drugs in September 2026, and about 80% of patients on Lilly's obesity pill were new to the drug class. Pills are therefore adding patients more than they are replacing injections.

What would change my view.

Worse

  • RTU cartridge prices slipping before 2028 (cartridges are the one format still fully booked)
  • The oral share of US obesity-drug prescriptions rising well beyond today's 10%
  • A multi-dose pen from Lilly in the United States

Better

  • Glass-syringe utilisation returning toward 95%
  • Evidence that Gerresheimer's troubles are sending vial customers to SCHOTT Pharma, a gain the model does not count

Score: 66, set by the Rater. Structural, non-cyclical volume forces (a 9% value market on biologics, obesity injectables and RTU conversion under 5% penetrated, Annex 1, the FDA draft guidance and BIOSECURE, destocking over) reach nearly all of sales and give about 7-8% volume and mix, net of a direct price give already visible where capacity is loose (RTU vials halved, bulk renewals -5-10%), synchronised syringe capacity from 2028, shrinking vaccines and unhedged currency; consensus sales growth at the 72nd percentile is honest. I sit above the group's 58 because the volume legs are structural and touch the whole business, but below Eckert & Ziegler because the environment supplies no price and its threats fall inside the three-year window.

#2 Internally-driven corporate change Score 52

Bottom line. Internal change at SCHOTT Pharma is real but narrow and financial. The change is enough to make the cash inflection credible, and not enough to lift earnings power unless the new plants fill.

Evidence. SCHOTT Pharma's leadership changed almost completely in nine months, and the new finance director has already delivered on cash. Reinhard Mayer, finance director since August 2025 and previously at two listed companies, has restructured the borrowing from the parent, lifted nine-month free cash flow by 49% and launched an efficiency programme of a "double-digit million euro" amount. The annual bonus now puts a 30% weight on operating free cash flow. Christian Mias, chief executive since May 2026 after 18 years inside the SCHOTT group, settled the dispute with the syringe customer within ten weeks and confirmed the medium-term targets. Against those gains, the most senior commercial executive left for a direct competitor, BD (Becton Dickinson), and his successor also runs the DCS segment.

The strategy has not changed: convert bulk containers to high-value formats, build capacity near customers, and partner on devices instead of owning them. There is no acquisition, no disposal and no buyback, and the dividend is 10% to 20% of earnings.

Three internal items deserve more weight than the market gives them.

  • Restraint on capital spending is already demonstrated. The US$371m syringe plant in North Carolina, announced in 2024, is still "under evaluation" with no final decision, and management is discussing a cheaper route: a syringe line at SCHOTT Pharma's existing site in Pennsylvania. Management says capital spending peaks in FY2027 and falls after.
  • The polymer problem is not yet addressed. The polymer-syringe lines built for mRNA vaccines are under-used, a programme to triple polymer capacity by 2027 is still running, and qualifying a new use for a line takes two to three years. The model credits only EUR 2m to 3m a year of recovery.
  • A listing of the Indian joint venture is an option that no forecast carries (box below). The joint venture is 50% owned and earned EUR 24m of net income in FY2025. A listing would also force the venture's dividend policy into the open. Today the venture pays SCHOTT Pharma little or nothing in cash, so EUR 11m to 14m of SCHOTT Pharma's EBITDA each year is not cash.
An option no forecast carries · low confidence (one press report, 21 October 2026)

Inference. The change at SCHOTT Pharma is financial discipline applied to an unchanged strategy. The change is not large enough to step up earnings power. The large positive, filling the new production lines, is the payoff of investment decisions taken in 2021 to 2024, and the new team will be judged on that payoff. The discipline is worth three things:

EUR 10m to 13mof EBITDA by FY2029 after wage inflation, about one point of margin
about EUR 0.06of EPS from lower interest by FY2030
Lower capital spendinga credible fall after FY2027, the most valuable of the three

So what. Internal change makes the cash story believable and puts a floor of about one point under the margin. Internal change does not answer the two forces pressing on the case: there is no stated plan for the under-used polymer lines, and no stated stance on capacity discipline while the industry over-builds.

Where I differ from the market: delivery has become more reliable in finance, not yet in operations. Deutsche Bank raised its target multiple in October, citing "more reliable delivery". Meanwhile the underlying EBITDA margin fell during FY2026, from 29.1% in the first half to about 26.3% in the second (the fourth quarter is my estimate, as it is not yet reported), and the market narrative has not registered the fall. The market is also unaware of the possible Indian listing, and the North Carolina plant has dropped out of 2026 broker research.

Strongest counter-case. The new chief executive is an insider with six months of results. The departed commercial head knows every contract and now sells against them. Staff retention is missing its targets just when the plant ramp-ups need engineers. And under-absorption of polymer costs could deepen before it eases, as the rest of the new capacity is commissioned.

What would change my view. Better: a quantified, year-by-year efficiency plan; a decision to close or redeploy the polymer lines outright, which I estimate would release EUR 10m to 15m of fixed cost at the price of a write-down; a capital markets day with cash targets. Worse: a final commitment to North Carolina before the capacity already built is full; another senior commercial departure.

Score: 52, set by the Rater. A new CFO and CEO have brought financial discipline to an unchanged strategy: a double-digit-million efficiency programme (about one point of margin by FY2029), pay 30% on free cash flow, nine-month FCF +49%, the customer dispute settled and North Carolina held back, worth a credible capex fall; against that the top commercial executive left for BD, polymer under-use has no plan and retention is missing targets, and none of it steps up earnings power. Gently positive and incremental, like Shell's self-help, so a shade above neutral and above the group's 44, which weighed the earlier target cut that predates this team.

#3 Industry structure, competitive advantage, financial profile and management Score 63

Bottom line. SCHOTT Pharma's foundations are robust where survival and revenue are concerned (industry structure, customer lock-in, balance sheet, clean earnings) and only average where upside is concerned (pricing, returns on new capital, capital allocation, minority shareholders' rights).

Evidence on structure and position. The industry is a concentrated oligopoly in which buyers rarely switch. The top three suppliers hold over 60% of core containment. Changing a registered container takes from six months to five years, and the container is under 1% of a drug's cost, so buyers of approved drugs put quality and security of supply ahead of price. SCHOTT Pharma's parent controls 60% to 70% of the world's pharmaceutical glass tubing, which gives SCHOTT Pharma supply security and a cost edge. SCHOTT Pharma's audit record is clean, while Gerresheimer is under a regulator's accounting probe and Stevanato has reported weaknesses in its internal controls.

Evidence on the financial profile. SCHOTT Pharma is strong on margin and balance sheet and weak on the return from recent capital. EBIT rose about EUR 14m between FY2022 and FY2025 on about EUR 310m of net new capital, a pre-tax return of roughly 5%. The EBITDA margin is second only to Sartorius Stedim among SCHOTT Pharma's four named peers.

27% to 28%EBITDA margin, second among four named peers
about 18%return on capital employed, from 22% to 25% five years ago
about 5%pre-tax return on the EUR 310m of capital added FY2022 to FY2025
about ¼of net income turned into free cash flow, on average
0.4xnet debt to EBITDA; no adjustments to EBITDA or EPS

Evidence on management and governance. The management team is prudent, engineering-led and delivers capital projects on time. Management is candid in tone and thin in disclosure: it publishes no split of price and volume, no utilisation rate and no obesity-drug revenue. The targets set at the 2023 listing (growth of at least 10% and margins in the low 30s) were cut within 27 months to growth of 6% to 8% and a margin "towards 30%".

The parent's control limits minority shareholders. SCHOTT Pharma's legal form, a partnership limited by shares (KGaA), lets the parent appoint management. The parent also takes a 1.5% brand royalty, supplies the glass tubing and runs the treasury, and its 77% holding rules out a buyback.

Inference. SCHOTT Pharma's moat is a set of barriers more than a set of advantages. The barriers keep entrants out and keep existing volume in. The barriers do not help SCHOTT Pharma beat Stevanato or BD to a new award, and they do not set price. SCHOTT Pharma's position is strongest where growth is moderate (vials) and weakest where growth is fastest (obesity-drug syringes). Management's goals are not stretching, because they were lowered, and the culture is quality-first rather than commercially aggressive.

So what. SCHOTT Pharma has a high floor under revenue, which I put at 4% to 5% organic growth in most environments, and a low ceiling on what price can add to the margin. That combination is the profile of a good, capital-heavy compounder. SCHOTT Pharma is not West, which has price rises of 2% to 4% a year, capital spending of 6% to 8% of sales and a 30% return on invested capital. The difference from West matters for the fair multiple (#11).

Where I differ from the market. I agree with the narrative that SCHOTT Pharma is the best company in European drug containment. I add two qualifications that the market does not make. First, margin comparisons with Stevanato ignore joint-venture income, which adds about 1.5 points to SCHOTT Pharma's group margin with no revenue behind it. Second, investors are paying a premium for quality just as the industry structure is about to be tested, by capacity that every leader is adding at once and by two drug makers who decide most of the marginal volume.

Strongest counter-case: the structure cracks where it is already thin. Large buyers call SCHOTT Pharma's and Stevanato's syringes "functionally equivalent" and award contracts on proximity and availability. In addition, the parent's tubing contract and its EUR 412m of credit facilities both reach their terms in December 2027, and a 10% re-pricing of tubing would cost about 7% of EPS. I give a tubing re-pricing about a 10% chance, because the tubing market is in surplus and the contract renews automatically.

What would change my view. Better: a primary syringe award on a major new drug; any disclosed positive price contribution; returns on capital turning up in FY2028. Worse: a re-pricing of tubing; a quality failure on a new line, which would attack the one advantage that is not in doubt.

Score: 63, set by the Rater. Qualitatively a concentrated, registration-locked oligopoly (top three over 60%, switching takes months to years, container under 1% of drug cost, 97% repeat revenue) with first places in vials and ampoules, a parent tubing edge and a clean audit record, but the moat protects volume not price, syringe awards are contested as functionally equivalent, and management lowered its goals inside a parent-first KGaA; ROIC of 15.9% (84th percentile) flatters, because the capital added since FY2022 earns about 5% pre-tax and FCF is a quarter of net income. Coherent with the groups (68, 57, 56, 42): close to Carlsberg's strong structure with ordinary returns, above Helios Towers on predictability of revenue.

#4 Guidance: conservatism, proactivity and the record Score 45

Bottom line. SCHOTT Pharma's guidance is reliable and mildly conservative inside each year, but the company has no record of serial raises and is not managing consensus down. Guidance therefore supports predictability more than it supports upgrades.

Evidence. Inside a fiscal year SCHOTT Pharma guides carefully and reports cleanly. The company raises guidance only on hard evidence: it declined to raise after a strong first quarter of FY2026 because extra shifts had flattered that quarter. It pre-releases results that differ materially from guidance. In every year since the listing, the margin has landed inside or above the range first guided.

Across years the record is poor. The listing targets were cut, and consensus EPS for FY2027 has fallen 17% in twelve months, nearly all of it around the guidance reset of December 2025.

The one raise under the new team was mostly the compensation payment. In July 2026 FY2026 guidance moved from growth of 2% to 5% and a margin of about 27% to growth of 5% to 6% and a margin of 27% to 28%. About three-quarters of the raise to growth came from the compensation payment. On the margin, the payment added about one point and the earlier write-down had cost about one point, so the underlying margin guidance moved by only about half a point.

Management's three named margin levers add up to the whole medium-term target, with nothing deducted. Three more points of high-value mix are worth about 30 basis points of margin. The end of ramp-up costs in Hungary and Serbia is worth 80 to 130 basis points. The efficiency programme is worth about 100 basis points. The sum, 210 to 260 basis points, is the whole distance from today's margin to "towards 30%". Nothing is deducted for wage inflation, for the start-up of the new Hungarian cartridge plant or for any price concession.

Inference. SCHOTT Pharma's guidance is conservative inside the year and not conservative on the medium-term margin. The company is also not keeping the sell-side's expectations low. The consensus margin for FY2027 (28.1%) sits above where I expect the guidance, and the lack of disclosure on drivers stops brokers from building cautious models from the parts. Against your three tests, SCHOTT Pharma passes on conservative current guidance, fails on keeping expectations conservative, and has too short and mixed a record on raising guidance.

What I expect on 10 December, and across the seven earnings events to May 2028. I expect FY2026 to be delivered in the upper half of its range, and FY2027 to be guided as shown below. The model's base case sits inside that expected guidance: in the lower half on growth and at the top on margin. A raise to growth guidance is unlikely even in a good year, because the one-offs in FY2026 force reported growth of about 8% in the first half of FY2027 and about 3% in the second.

Where I differ from the market: on the medium-term target, not on FY2027. For FY2027 I agree with Deutsche Bank, which expects guidance for growth of 5% to 7%. FactSet's median still implies 6.0% growth and a 28.1% margin, so the guidance can read slightly soft on the day while matching what the informed brokers already expect. My difference is on the medium-term target. The four brokers who forecast FY2029 have a 29.3% margin, which treats "towards 30%" as a commitment. I read "towards 30%" as elastic wording that a 29% margin would satisfy, which makes a formal cut to the target unlikely and a shortfall against brokers' numbers likely.

Strongest counter-case. In favour of more conservatism than I assume: the December 2025 guidance proved conservative even without the compensation (underlying growth of about 4.5% against a range of 2% to 5%), so FY2027 could be the first genuine beat-and-raise year. Against: a fourth-quarter underlying margin near 26% may lead the new chief executive to guide "around 27%" and reset expectations once more.

What would change my view. A FY2027 margin range that reaches 29% would be a bull signal. A range centred below 27.5% would be a bear signal.

Score: 45, set by the Rater. Inside each year guidance is careful and every margin range since listing was met or beaten, but the listing targets were cut within 27 months, FY2027 consensus EPS fell 17% around the December 2025 reset, the one raise was mostly the compensation payment, and the company is not keeping consensus low (FY2027 consensus margin 28.1% above the likely guide, the medium-term 'towards 30%' likely missed). A mixed record with a recent medium-term cut, coherent with the groups (42, 45): below Sdiptech's untested new targets, above Instalco's miss of every target.

#5 Does revenue growth lead to outsized profit growth? Score 46

Bottom line. SCHOTT Pharma turns revenue growth into EPS growth about 1.5 times as fast, mostly because the lines below EBITDA have stopped rising. Anything more needs operating leverage that the company has not shown since the pandemic.

Evidence, lever by lever.

  • Operating leverage is real at the plant and diluted at the group. Extra volume through a plant already built earns 45 to 55 cents of EBITDA per euro of revenue. Since FY2022 the company has realised about 32 cents, because each new site adds staff, validation teams and start-up costs before it adds revenue. Single years have ranged from 10 to 77 cents, so only the multi-year figure is usable. At the EBIT level the leverage has been close to nil, because depreciation rose about 14% a year, from 6.7% to 8.5% of sales.
  • Pricing power is contractual and unused. Contracts index glass costs every six months and labour costs every February, so SCHOTT Pharma recovers inflation with a lag. There is no evidence of real price rises: gross margin has fallen from 36.0% in FY2022 to 31% to 33%. One point of like-for-like price is about EUR 11m of EBITDA and 5% of EPS. At SCHOTT Pharma, price is a risk, not a lever.
  • Financial leverage is negligible.
  • Cost-out is small (#2), because the company is expanding its footprint, not shrinking it.
  • Feedback loops run in both directions. In DCS a reinforcing loop is at work: lines fill, fixed costs are absorbed, and the extra cash funds the next RTU conversion. In DDS syringes a balancing loop is forming: every leader adds capacity, utilisation falls and tenders are discounted. Under both loops sits the slow loop that protects revenue: each new drug registered in a SCHOTT Pharma container is a 10- to 30-year annuity.

Inference: the leverage is lopsided. Revenue growth leads to outsized profit growth only on capacity already built. A volume shortfall on built capacity loses about half of the lost revenue as profit. A volume gain that needs new shifts or lines earns only about a third of the extra revenue as profit. Per point of volume, the downside is therefore about 1.5 times the upside.

The EPS bridge shows why EPS stalled and why EPS restarts. From FY2023 to FY2026 EBITDA rose EUR 48m, worth +EUR 0.24 a share, but depreciation took back EUR 0.21, the tax rate EUR 0.06 and interest EUR 0.01. In FY2027 EBITDA rises by the usual EUR 20m, but depreciation rises by only EUR 7.5m instead of EUR 14m to 18m, the tax rate eases and interest falls. The operations do not have to do anything new. The lines below EBITDA simply stop taking the growth away.

So what. "Outsized" profit growth at SCHOTT Pharma means EPS growing about 1.5 times as fast as revenue: +8% on revenue growth of +5.5% in FY2027, and about +10% on +6.5% after. That growth is worth having, but SCHOTT Pharma is not a geared story. From FY2028 the forecasts also require the realised conversion to rise from 32 cents of EBITDA per extra euro of revenue to 36 cents.

Where I differ from the market: consensus for FY2028 assumes nearly the full plant-level conversion. Brokers frame FY2027 as a margin recovery, and consensus for FY2028 implies about 42 cents of EBITDA per extra euro of revenue (EUR 32m on EUR 76m). That rate is close to the full plant-level rate, as if no new fixed cost arrived in the year the Hungarian cartridge plant starts up. I think 36 cents is the right centre.

Strongest counter-case. The bulls' version: the leverage is latent and large. The DDS margin has fallen from over 35% to about 31.5%, and each point of DDS margin is worth 2.3% of EPS. If the optimisation costs end and the polymer lines refill, the DDS margin snaps back faster than any model shows. The bears' version: price falls first, drops through to profit in full, and swamps the gain from absorbing fixed costs (#9, judgement 3).

What would change my view. A first-quarter FY2027 DDS margin above 31% and a group margin above 28% (results in February 2027) would support the bulls. A DDS margin below 29% with revenue growing would show that the layer of fixed costs is still outrunning volume.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. The structure has plant-level drop-through of 45-55 cents per euro but has realised only about 32 cents since FY2022 as each new site adds fixed cost first, with EBIT leverage near nil as depreciation rose to 8.5% of sales; pricing is index pass-through with no real price taken (gross margin down from 36%), financial leverage is negligible, cost-out is small, and the DCS absorption loop is offset by a balancing capacity loop in DDS syringes. EPS grows about 1.5 times revenue, below the median company's twice, and the gearing is asymmetric (downside about 1.5 times upside) with no pricing power behind it, so just below ordinary, coherent with the groups (56, 47).

#6 Forecast financials Score 68

Bottom line. The forecasts show EPS growth returning at 8% in FY2027 and then about 10% a year, with free cash flow more than doubling by FY2029. The forecasts are better than the past on earnings and cash, about 5% below consensus on EPS, and dependent on the margin having bottomed in the second half of FY2026.

The two free-cash-flow rows differ because the model has no line for joint-venture profit that is booked but not paid out in cash. I use the lower row. Net debt, on the company's definition, is about EUR 104m at September 2026 and turns to net cash in FY2029.

The scope for double-digit growth is in EPS from FY2028, not in revenue. From FY2027 to FY2030 revenue compounds at about 6% a year, EBITDA at about 8% and EPS at about 10%.

Against the past, the next four years are better on earnings and cash and no better on growth. Revenue grows more slowly than in FY2020 to FY2025 (11% a year, including the pandemic) and about as fast as in FY2022 to FY2025. The EBITDA margin ends 1.5 to 2 points higher than today, which is about a year later and a point lower than the company's target. EPS goes from no growth to about 10% a year. Free cash flow rises from about a quarter of net income to about 70% by FY2030. SCHOTT Pharma is therefore an execution-and-cash case, not a growth or pricing case.

Where the EPS growth comes from. Of the EUR 0.43 gain in EPS from FY2025 to FY2030, about 60% is EBITDA growth net of depreciation (volume through built capacity, and mix), about 15% is the falling interest charge, and the rest is revenue growth at a constant margin.

The reported quarters of FY2027 will mislead. Because of the one-offs in the FY2026 base, reported revenue growth in the four quarters of FY2027 should run at about +6.5%, +10%, +4.5% and +1.5%. The change in margin against a year earlier should be about flat, +180, +200 and -260 basis points. Compare each quarter with the quarter before, on an underlying basis.

Reported results will flatter in May and August 2027 and disappoint in December 2027, with no change in the underlying trend.

Where I differ from the market: consensus has the right shape and runs about a year early on margin. On revenue there is no difference. On EBITDA the model is 1% to 3% lower. On EPS the model is about 5% lower in FY2027 and FY2028, and more than half of the FY2027 gap sits below EBITDA: consensus implies an interest charge of about EUR 4m, while SCHOTT Pharma's debt supports about EUR 7.5m. On free cash flow the model is well below consensus in FY2027 and FY2028 and level in FY2029, despite lower earnings.

Strongest counter-case. Consensus is right: the second half of FY2026 was a low point depressed by temporary costs, and the margin is back at 28% by the first quarter of FY2027. On the other side, the run-rate case gives a fifth year of flat EPS (#9, judgement 1).

What would change my view. The first-quarter FY2027 margin, reported in February 2027, settles most of the question either way.

Score: 68, set by the Rater. 9.6% falls in the 5-10% C band, just short of B; I place it high in the band because the growth is wholly organic and the margin path rises 1.5-2 points to 29.3%, above any year since FY2022, with a mechanical lift below EBITDA, held off the top because it depends on the FY2026 second-half margin being the low point and sits about 5% below consensus.

#7 Scope for upgrades over the coming 6 to 12 months Score 35

Bottom line. Over the next six months the scope is for small downgrades to EPS and a larger downgrade to FY2027 free cash flow. The first real scope for upgrades, in cash and in the narrative, arrives in the second half of 2027.

Evidence. Consensus consists of two groups of brokers. The three with the deepest published work (UBS, Deutsche Bank and Jefferies) have FY2027 EPS of EUR 1.04 to 1.06 and FY2028 EPS of EUR 1.15 to 1.19. The other seven are at EUR 1.07 to 1.16 and EUR 1.20 to 1.31. Six of the ten estimates predate October. Consensus capital spending for FY2027 is below FY2026, the opposite of what management has said, and consensus holds capital spending flat at EUR 153m in FY2028 and FY2029.

Inference, line by line.

  • Guidance: met, not raised (#4).
  • Consensus EPS: trimmed. I expect the FY2027 median to move to EUR 1.06 to 1.08 by February 2027 and the FY2028 median to EUR 1.18 to 1.20 within a year. I put the chance that FY2027 consensus EPS is lower by February at 60%, unchanged at 30% and higher at 10%.
  • Consensus free cash flow for FY2027: cut by a quarter or more, which I put at 75% likely by February.
  • Consensus free cash flow for FY2028 and FY2029: the one line with upgrades in view. If the company confirms falling capital spending in December 2027, the FY2029 figure rises by EUR 15m to 20m. I put that upgrade at about 50% likely, held back by the open decision on North Carolina.
  • Breadth of revisions: negative from December 2026 to February 2027, flat to positive from May to August 2027 while the reported comparisons flatter, and at risk again in December 2027 (timeline below).
  • Narrative: the market narrative has moved three times in a year, from "credibility crisis" to "past the trough" to "obesity-drug contract risk". The next constructive narrative, "mechanical EPS growth plus a cash inflection, heading to net cash", has no dated trigger before December 2027.
Not yet skewed to upgrades: small EPS downgrades in the next three months; the first real scope for upgrades, in cash, comes in December 2027.

So what: the scope for upgrades in the next six months is low, but the sequence of revisions is useful. The coming downgrade is small, dated (10 December to February) and already visible in the fresh estimates. After the downgrade, the calendar turns helpful for two reporting seasons. December 2027 then offers the first guidance day since the listing on which growth, margin and capital spending could all point the right way off a clean base. A situation skewed to upgrades may be forming for the second half of 2027. That situation is not here now.

Where I differ from the market: the gap is between a stale median and the fresh estimates, and the model stands with the fresh estimates. Nowhere on the profit-and-loss account is the model above consensus. The only line on which the model is above consensus is free cash flow from FY2029. Target prices average EUR 25. Target prices rose 32% in six months while EPS estimates rose 3%, and I expect target prices to converge on EUR 22 to 24 after guidance that reads soft.

Strongest counter-case. Upgrades could come early: a first-half FY2027 DDS margin above 32% and a group margin above 28% (about a one-in-four chance) would confirm consensus and restart the rise in target prices. Or the cuts could be larger: a fourth-quarter underlying margin near 26% is taken as a run-rate, and FY2027 consensus EPS falls 6% to 8%.

What would change my view. Guidance for FY2027 capital spending at or below EUR 150m, together with margin guidance of "around 28%", would remove most of the expected trim.

Score: 35, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely to be met not raised on 10 December (one margin raise at most, about one in three, against a 15-20% chance of a cut); consensus EPS, a stale median above the fresh brokers, is 60% likely to be trimmed 2-4% by February, about -0.5 times 5.5% revenue growth, and FY2027 FCF consensus is likely cut by a quarter, while the narrative has no dated positive before December 2027, just outside the window. Below the group's 44 because the trim is likely and sizeable against slow growth, lifted a little by flat-to-positive breadth in May-August 2027: above TT Electronics, below IMCD.

#8 Current momentum, for the stock and its peers Score 72

Bottom line. SCHOTT Pharma's momentum is real over six months but has stalled since October, and the momentum was built on higher multiples rather than on earnings upgrades. The peer group is split between rewarded pricing power and penalised glass capacity, and SCHOTT Pharma is the best of the penalised group.

Evidence for the stock. The dashboard's pinned ratings (snapshot of 11 November 2026) are A for technical momentum, A for sell-side earnings momentum, B for valuation and C for thematic fit and momentum. The parts under those letters are weaker than the letters:

  • Price. EUR 21.4 in the snapshot, which is 11% below the 50-day average and 13% above the 200-day average. Returns are -2.5% over three months and +33% over six. The 200-day average has risen in only four of the last twelve months.
  • Estimates. Consensus EPS for FY2027 has moved 0%, +2% and +3% over one, three and six months, against +1%, +21% and +32% for target prices (chart below). The share of buy ratings is 46%, down 23 points in a month.
  • Guidance. One raise in twelve months, most of it mechanical (#4).

Evidence for peers: the peer group has split in two. Suppliers with pricing power or device lock-in are beating forecasts and raising guidance: West (organic growth of 11.9%, full-year guidance raised, about 38 times earnings) and Ypsomed (guidance raised on 11 November). The glass and capacity names are being marked down: Stevanato (-28% in a day) and Gerresheimer (earnings momentum F, 10.3 times earnings, at the 4th percentile of its own history, 8% buy ratings). In the dashboard's sector, only SCHOTT Pharma and GVS hold an A for earnings momentum, and nine of the other twelve stocks hold a D or an F.

Inference: momentum is paused, not strong. The stock's A for sell-side momentum is a composite that hides its parts. The upgrade cycle of 2026 was in target prices and multiples, not in earnings, and the cycle has stopped. The earnings part of sell-side momentum is about to turn slightly negative (#7). The A for technical momentum reflects a six-month rise, but the price has since broken below its 50-day average.

Among peers the market is paying for pricing power and marking down glass capacity. SCHOTT Pharma's position as the best of the marked-down group is a relative strength, and the same position is why the stock fell with Stevanato.

One measurement sharpens the picture: the stock gets full credit for its own delivery and no shelter from the industry's shocks. Over the last six months the peer basket explains only 12% of the stock's daily moves. About nine-tenths of the 34% rise came from a higher multiple earned on the company's own events. The one sharp fall came from an industry event at a peer.

#9 Riskiness and simplicity of the forecasts Score 57

Bottom line. The case is simple and trackable in its central path and fragile in a narrow, nameable place: price, one customer and one segment's margin. Because of the thin free float, the risk to the share price is larger than the risk to the business.

How simple the case is. The case is simple in structure: one industry, two segments, unadjusted earnings and a constant 150.6m shares. EUR 10m of EBITDA is EUR 7.75m of net income at a 22.5% tax rate, which is EUR 0.051 a share, or about 5% of EPS. The case is concentrated in its drivers: absorption of built capacity, like-for-like price and the DDS margin are one driver seen from three sides.

The range of outcomes: balanced around the model, skewed negative against consensus. For FY2027 my 80% ranges are revenue within about 3% either way, EBITDA within about 5%, EPS of EUR 0.96 to 1.12, and free cash flow of EUR 30m to 80m. For FY2028, the 80% range for EPS is EUR 1.00 to 1.30. Around the model's base case, the body of the range is balanced and the tail is to the downside. Against consensus the skew is clearly negative: consensus EPS for FY2027 sits at about the 80th percentile of my range.

The five judgements, worked step by step. Price and the Lilly relationship move EPS most.

Judgement 1: the second half of FY2026 was the low point for the margin.

  1. FY2027 revenue of EUR 1,099m at a 27.9% margin gives EBITDA of EUR 307m.
  2. At a 27.0% margin, the gap is 0.9 points x EUR 1,099m = EUR 9.9m of EBITDA.
  3. Pre-tax profit falls from EUR 203.2m to EUR 193.3m, net income from EUR 157.5m to EUR 149.8m, and EPS from EUR 1.05 to EUR 0.99, which is -5%.
  4. If the second half's margin of about 26.3% is a run-rate, the gap is 1.6 points x EUR 1,099m = EUR 17.6m. EPS is then EUR 0.96, which is -9% and below FY2026. Free cash flow falls by EUR 8m to 14m.
  5. If the margin shortfall persists into the calendar-2029 earnings on which the 18-month valuation rests, the shortfall takes about 4.5% off the value at any multiple.
  6. Upside: at a 28.5% margin, EBITDA is EUR 6.6m higher and EPS is EUR 1.08 (+3%).

My odds: the second half of FY2026 was the low point, about 60%; something in between, about 25%; a run-rate, about 15%.

Judgement 2: more of the growth runs through plants already built.

  1. From FY2027 to FY2030 revenue rises by EUR 222m and EBITDA by EUR 81m, a conversion of 36 cents per euro.
  2. At the 32 cents realised since FY2022, 0.32 x EUR 222m = EUR 71m. FY2030 EBITDA is then EUR 9.4m lower, the margin is 28.6% and EPS is EUR 1.35 (-3.5%).
  3. At 27 cents, if new capacity keeps arriving ahead of volume, FY2030 EBITDA is EUR 20.6m lower, the margin is 27.7% and EPS is EUR 1.30 (-7.6%).
  4. At the 42 cents that consensus needs, FY2030 EBITDA is EUR 12.8m higher, the margin is 30.3% and EPS is EUR 1.47 (+4.7%).

The surprise is how modest the effects of conversion are. The pace of absorption matters less than the next two judgements.

Judgement 3: like-for-like price stays flat.

  1. One point of price on FY2028 revenue of EUR 1,171m is EUR 11.7m, and the whole amount drops through to EBITDA.
  2. FY2028 EPS falls by 11.7 x 0.775 / 150.6 = EUR 0.06, to EUR 1.09 (-5%).
  3. A point a year for three years is about 3% of FY2030 revenue, or EUR 39.7m of EBITDA. FY2030 EPS is then EUR 1.20 instead of EUR 1.40 (-15%).
  4. The FY2030 margin is then 27.1%.

The earlier analysis puts the chance of such price falls at 25% to 30%, starting in FY2028, and I agree. Falling price is the largest fundamental risk, and it is the one risk that the company's disclosure cannot reveal directly.

One point of like-for-like price is 5% of EPS; a point a year for three years cancels the whole forecast margin gain.
FY2030 EBITDA margin29.3%→27.1%
FY2030 EPSEUR 1.40→EUR 1.20
EPS growth a yearabout 10%→4% to 5%

Judgement 4: Eli Lilly makes no volume or format cut.

  1. Obesity-drug revenue in FY2028 is about EUR 165m (derived), and two-thirds of it, about EUR 110m or 9% of sales, is with Lilly. An unnamed customer was 10.3% of first-half FY2026 sales; if that customer is Lilly, including insulin and vials, the exposure is about a quarter larger.
  2. A 30% cut is EUR 33m of revenue. On built capacity about half of the lost revenue is lost as profit: EUR 16.5m of EBITDA, or EUR 0.085 of EPS (-7%).
  3. A 50% cut is EUR 55m of revenue, EUR 27.5m of EBITDA and EUR 0.14 of EPS (-12%). Revenue growth in that year falls from 6.5% to between 2% and 4%.
  4. Take-or-pay compensation returns part of the loss two to three quarters later, as it did in FY2026.
  5. A format shift works the same way: if a fifth of the syringe volume moved to multi-dose pens, about EUR 22m of revenue and 5% of EPS would go.

I put the chance of a Lilly event in the next 18 months at 15% to 20%. Customers set such cuts in their summer budget round, so a cut for FY2028 would surface between July and December 2027.

Judgement 5: capital spending falls after FY2027.

  1. Base free cash flow is EUR 94m in FY2028, EUR 127m in FY2029 and EUR 149m in FY2030. The FY2029 figure is 4.0% of today's market value.
  2. Committing to North Carolina (about EUR 330m) adds EUR 40m to 60m a year of capital spending, which gives FY2029 free cash flow of EUR 67m to 87m and no net cash.
  3. EPS is untouched until the plant starts to depreciate. On a 15-year life, my assumption, depreciation is about EUR 22m a year, or EUR 0.11 a share (about 8% of EPS), before any revenue from the plant.
  4. Milder version: capital spending stays at EUR 145m instead of falling to EUR 135m. The milder version costs EUR 10m a year of free cash flow and still beats consensus.

I put a commitment to North Carolina by the end of FY2028 at about one in three.

The risks cluster. A customer cut lowers utilisation and invites price concessions at the next contract renewal. A customer cut and a price concession together could take 15% to 20% off FY2028 EPS.

Suddenness and trackability: the risk gathers on two guidance days, and three quarterly reports test the thesis within six months. Inside a fiscal year the company has been predictable. The two guidance days are 10 December 2026 and December 2027. Each of the three quarterly reports due within six months carries the number that tests the thesis soonest.

The limit of this tracking is diagnosis. If a margin disappoints, nothing the company publishes says whether the cause is price, which would break the thesis, or absorption of fixed costs, which would only delay it.

Share-price risk beyond the fundamentals is large. With an 18% free float and a few million dollars traded a day, sector news moves the stock 10% to 20%. The precedents are large: Stevanato lost 28% in a day; West lost 40% in February 2025 on guidance 18% below consensus; and SCHOTT Pharma's own reset of December 2025 took its multiple to 11.7x.

Sector precedent places SCHOTT Pharma between the successes and the failures, which is where the base case sits. Demand is not cyclical. The cycles are in customers' stock levels (2022 to 2025) and in industry capacity (2027 to 2030). Underperformance in this industry has come from three patterns: a spending peak that runs ahead of utilisation, a single-customer shock, and a failure of leverage or governance. SCHOTT Pharma is exposed to the first two patterns and not the third.

Of seven attempts by comparable companies to lift margins out of a spending peak, two succeeded on time, and each of the two had a lever that SCHOTT Pharma lacks: West had price and GVS had plant closures. Three were late, all with greenfield plants and concentrated customers. The other two attempts are SCHOTT Pharma's own: success in the pandemic shortage, and no progress at EBIT since. SCHOTT Pharma's current expansions are at existing sites and its one greenfield plant is deferred. The base case therefore assumes margin gains that are real, about half the size consensus assumes, and a year late.

Where I differ from the market. Investors fear contract risk in obesity drugs more than the sell-side does. For FY2027 I am with the sell-side, and for 2028 to 2030 I am with the investors (#1). Three risks appear in nobody's commentary: the customer at 10.3% of sales, the parent contracts that expire in December 2027, and the joint-venture profit that is not received in cash.

Strongest counter-case: I understate the simplicity. Revenue is 97% repeat, prices are locked for three years, the earnings have no adjustments, and a wrong base case shows within one quarter.

What would change my view. Any disclosure of price against volume, or of utilisation, would make the case much easier to diagnose and would lower its risk at a stroke.

Score: 57, set by the Rater. The structure is simple (unadjusted earnings, constant share count, net debt 0.2x EBITDA, non-cyclical demand, 97% repeat revenue) and the FY2027 EPS cone of EUR 0.96-1.12 is about 8% either way, but FY2028 widens to about 13%, the drivers are one driver seen three ways (absorption, renewal price, DDS margin) that the company's disclosure cannot separate, a customer event at Lilly (15-20% odds) is sudden and clusters with price to 15-20% of FY2028 EPS, and an 18% float passes sector news through as 10-20% moves. Between the groups' 40 and 60; below Banca Generali's narrow range, a little above NKT's concentrated execution risk.

#10 Where the stock is in its lifecycle Score 59

Bottom line. The stock is turning up and has not yet broadened. May 2027 is the earliest, and December 2027 the likeliest, point at which the evidence for broadening can be in hand.

Evidence. The dashboard's rule puts the stock's starting phase at Broadening. The path so far: a collapse through 2025; a bottom in February to March 2026 at 11.7x; a turn in July 2026 on a volume beat, the customer settlement and a broker upgrade; a peak at 20.8x on 22 October; and a fall to 17.4x after Stevanato's warning.

The dashboard's rule appears to have read the stock at its autumn high. The Phases page shows a multiple "now" of 20.4x, which is the September month-end reading. At today's price the multiple is 17.4x on consensus EPS and 18.9x on the model's EPS.

Inference: the stock is turning up, and a first attempt at broadening has been interrupted. Broadening would show as estimates rising across lines, guidance raised on fundamentals, more brokers turning positive, and the thesis widening from "past the trough" to "operating leverage and cash". The evidence instead shows EPS estimates up 2% to 3% in six months, one largely mechanical raise, a buy share that has just fallen to 46%, and a lead broker back at Hold. The next revisions are more likely down than up (#7).

The stock is not stalling either. The turn in volume is real, the company's own numbers have not deteriorated, and mechanical EPS growth lies ahead.

So what: the route from turning up to broadening is dated. The route runs through the fourth-quarter margin and the guidance (10 December), the first-quarter DDS margin (February 2027), the first half (May 2027), and then a clean FY2028 guide with lower capital spending (December 2027).

Where I differ from the market. The dashboard's rule, and the brokers who raised their target multiples in October, treat the recovery as established. Investors have since marked the recovery down. I sit between the two: the turn is established, and the broadening is not.

Strongest counter-case. For Broadening: twelve-month price momentum, A ratings for technical and sell-side momentum, and a FY2027 that will print EPS growth after four flat years. For Stalling: the July raise was mechanical, the underlying margin fell through FY2026, and soft guidance is coming.

What would change my view. A group margin above 28% in February with unchanged estimates would move me to Broadening by May. A fourth-quarter underlying margin of 26% or less, with guidance centred below 27.5%, would move me to Stalling.

Score: 59, set by the Rater. The computed Broadening reads the autumn high; I agree with the memo that the stock turned up in July 2026 (volume beat, settlement, mechanical EPS growth ahead) and has not broadened: EPS estimates up only 2-3% in six months, one mechanical raise, the buy share falling and the next revisions more likely down, with broadening confirmable from May 2027 at the earliest. Turning up but past its early stage and paused, so like Nexans' paused momentum and above Greggs' bottoming.

#11 The fair multiple Score 62

Bottom line. The guideline multiple of 23.3x is fair for a Broadening phase that the stock has not yet entered, and the market has paid 23.3x only for the listing-era promise. I therefore treat 23.3x as the upper end of the range for the end of 2027, and about 20x as the centre.

The guideline. 23.32x two-year-forward earnings, the 80th percentile of the stock's own history, set for the Broadening phase.

My view: 23.3x is the top of the plausible range at the end of 2027, not its centre. My centre is about 20x, for four reasons.

  1. The history is short and front-loaded with the listing-era promise. The stock has 35 months of data. The guideline therefore asks the market to pay again a multiple it has only ever paid for a promise the company no longer makes (callout below).
  2. The phase. If the stock is turning up and not yet broadening (#10), your own framework points lower in the range, because the forecasts are less certain.
  3. The quality of what is capitalised. A top-quintile multiple suits a business with price and high returns on new capital. SCHOTT Pharma has 10% EPS growth with no price lever, about 5% returns on the capital it added from FY2022 to FY2025, and free cash flow that even in FY2029 is only about two-thirds of net income. At 23.3x earnings the shares would trade at about 36 times FY2029 free cash flow.
  4. The structure. An 18% free float and the KGaA legal form keep many institutions out. Deutsche Bank, which calls the stock close to un-investable for large funds, uses a 22x target multiple and rates the stock Hold.
Every month at or above the 23.3x guideline fell between December 2023 and August 2024, in the first year after listing, when the company was promising growth of at least 10% and margins in the low 30s. Those targets were withdrawn in December 2025. Since August 2024 the highest month-end reading is 22.4x; the 2026 peak was 20.8x.

Where the stock is now: the guideline needs a larger re-rating than the Phases page shows. The re-rating to the guideline is 23% from the model's 18.9x and about a third from 17.4x on consensus EPS, not the 14% the Phases page shows. For reference, the stock's ten-year bands on the dashboard are 13.6x (10th percentile), 17.1x (35th), 18.8x (median) and 22.4x (75th).

Where I differ from the market. At 17.4x the market is paying a little under the median multiple for a recovery it has just marked down. Broker targets average EUR 25, which is about 20 times consensus two-year-forward EPS. I am close to the brokers on where the multiple could reach if FY2027 delivers, and below the guideline.

Strongest counter-case for a higher multiple. Revenue is non-cyclical and 97% repeat. Earnings are unadjusted. The balance sheet is heading to net cash. The median of the history includes a credibility crisis that has passed. A thin float amplifies rallies as well as falls. And if the Indian joint venture lists, part of the earnings base is revalued (#2). In a year in which EPS grows 10%, cash flow doubles and guidance is finally raised, a multiple of 22x to 23x is defensible.

What would change my view. Up: a first-half FY2027 DDS margin of 32% or more; a FY2028 guide with capital spending of EUR 145m or less; price holding on renewals; or the parent acting to widen the free float. Down: visible price concessions, a commitment to North Carolina, or a customer event.

Score: 62, set by the Rater. Neutral on both gives C; both readings predate the 3 November fall, and at today's 17.4x consensus (18.9x the model's) the stock sits nearer the 40th percentile of its short history, so the readings lean cheap. I place it in the upper half but not higher, because a turning-up, not-yet-broadening phase, about 5% returns on new capital and a short history inflated by listing-era promises deserve a multiple near the median rather than the guideline 23.3x.

  • Dividends and other cash returns (under 1% a year). The payout ratio is about 18% and there is no buyback. Cash returns become a live question in FY2029, when net cash builds at EUR 90m to 115m a year with no stated use. A 40% payout on FY2029 earnings would be about EUR 0.51 a share, a 2.4% yield on today's price. The alternative use of the cash is the North Carolina plant.

The return to 31 December 2027 at other multiples and earnings (my arithmetic: the multiple times two-year-forward EPS of EUR 1.31, plus EUR 0.36 of dividends, against a price of EUR 21.15).

Reading the grid: the earnings alone carry a reasonable return, and the model's headline needs the multiple. With no re-rating, the forecasts alone give +18% to +19% to the end of 2027, and about +34% (12% a year) to mid-2029, if FY2029 and FY2030 arrive as forecast. My weights are about 25% on the guideline outcome, 40% on about 20x, 20% on no re-rating, and 15% on a de-rating with lower earnings. The weights give an expected return of about +20% to the end of 2027, with about one chance in seven of losing a fifth or more.

about +20%my weighted expected return to the end of 2027
1 in 7chance of losing a fifth or more
+46%the model's headline at 23.3x, about half of it the multiple

Where I differ from the market. Broker targets imply about +18% plus the dividend, close to my weighted figure. The model's +46% is well above both, and the whole difference is the multiple.

Strongest counter-case: the multiple and the earnings are not independent. The outcomes that deliver FY2029 EPS (margins rising, price holding, capital spending falling) are the same outcomes that would earn 22x to 23x, so the upper-right corner of the grid is more likely than separate odds suggest. The same link works in the lower-left corner.

What would change my view. The dated tests in #9. By May 2027 the weights should have moved decisively one way.

Score: 75, set by the Rater. About +20-22% sits at the floor of the B band, and the three-year check is supportive; I hold it at the floor because half the model's headline is re-rating, the earnings part rests on FY2029-FY2030, and the lower tail is fat (about one chance in seven of losing a fifth or more).

#13 Summary conclusion

SCHOTT Pharma is a good business coming out of a bad four years. The franchise was never in question: lock-in, an oligopoly and the parent's tubing kept revenue growing through a vaccine collapse, a destocking and a customer cut. What failed was the conversion of capital into earnings. That conversion is now set to improve for reasons that are mostly arithmetic: depreciation, tax and interest stop rising faster than EBITDA, and capital spending falls after FY2027. On the base case the improvement gives EPS growth of 8% and then about 10% a year, and free cash flow that more than doubles by FY2029, with nothing required that the company has not already shown.

What the case lacks today is a positive skew in revisions. Consensus is a few percent too high, guidance will be met and not raised, and the narrative holds no dated positive before December 2027. What the case has is a small and visible downside to estimates, a concentrated and trackable set of risks, and a return that is positive across most combinations of multiple and earnings.

The practical question is one of timing against evidence. The estimate reset comes in the next three months. The first hard test of the margin comes in February 2027, and the first day on which guidance, estimates and narrative could all move up together is December 2027.

Acting before the evidence

  • Captures the re-rating that the evidence would bring
  • Carries the estimate reset of December 2026 to February 2027
  • Carries the Lilly customer risk and the thin free float without the evidence

Waiting for the evidence

  • First hard test: the first-quarter margin, February 2027
  • First possible joint upgrade of guidance, estimates and narrative: December 2027
  • Costs some of the re-rating

The one item that could move the timetable forward, and that nobody is discussing, is a listing of the Indian joint venture.

Thesis's Change Forces' Strength: 59, set by the Rater. Clearly positive but volume-only external forces (66) and a near-neutral, financial internal change (52) reach profits mostly mechanically, lifting EPS to about 10% a year (C, 68), a little below the Universe's median growth, with no pricing help and the strongest force, the cash inflection, dated for FY2028, so a mild net positive in the high 50s.

Foundations' Robustness: 70, set by the Rater. The foundations are robust where survival and revenue are concerned (a concentrated, registration-locked oligopoly, 97% repeat non-cyclical revenue, clean earnings, almost no debt), which carries the business above its quality score of 63, but no pricing power, falling margins, weak returns on new capital, parent-first governance and a mixed delivery record (45) keep it below the stable, price-setting franchises at 75-80.

Setups' Fit/Crispness: 67, set by the Rater. The case fits a cause for concern clearing in a good, low-cyclicality business in substance (capacity built ahead of demand stalled EPS, and the stall now ends mechanically as depreciation, tax and interest stop absorbing EBITDA and capex peaks), but today's problems blur it: the underlying margin was still falling in the second half of FY2026, polymer lines are unaddressed and a second concern (obesity-drug contracts and format) has just opened; how much is already in the price is left to topics 7 and 12.

Case Riskiness: 55, set by the Rater. The central path is simple, trackable and low in financial and cyclical risk (topic 9 at 57), but the risks are not paper cuts: renewal price (25-30% odds, up to -15% of FY2030 EPS) and a Lilly volume event cluster in one undiagnosable margin line, the company is not managing consensus down, and the 18% float turns sector news into 10-20% moves, so just above typical.
